paper_a.title: Similarity Estimation Techniques from Rounding Algorithms

paper_b.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor: Towards Removing the Curse of Dimensionality

metadata.description: Both papers center on the locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) framework. Paper A (Charikar 2002, SimHash) introduces a new LSH definition based on sim(x,y) = Pr[h(x)=h(y)] and constructs LSH families for cosine/angular similarity (random hyperplanes), Jaccard (min-wise), and EMD (Kleinberg-Tardos rounding). Paper B (Har-Peled-Indyk-Motwani 2012, the journal version of the original LSH paper) defines (r1,r2,p1,p2)-sensitive families and proves the canonical LSH-based (c,r)-NN data-structure theorem with rho = log(1/p1)/log(1/p2). Both papers reprove the same Hamming-cube approximate NN result via concatenated LSH bits. Relation type is SM (same method): the LSH framework is the shared technique, applied to similarity sketching (A) versus nearest-neighbor data structures (B). NOTE: both papers carry registry_mismatch_note swaps but the actual content matches the LSH vs SimHash pair.
metadata.registry_note: Both papers carry registry_mismatch_note flags but in a complementary swap: paper309's PDF is Charikar 2002 (SimHash), paper310's PDF is Har-Peled-Indyk-Motwani 2012 (LSH/ANN). The pair is therefore intact under this swap; alignment proceeds. Both extracted via PDF->text fallback so `medium`-confidence dominates.

matches.explanation: Both papers define a locality-sensitive hash family. Paper A gives Charikar's collision-equals-similarity definition (DP309.1) and reproduces the Indyk-Motwani parameter-based variant (DP309.2: (r1,r2,p1,p2)-sensitive); paper B uses exactly the (r1,r2,p1,p2)-sensitive definition (DP310.5). DP309.2 is tagged origin=external citing Indyk-Motwani [31], which is precisely paper B's tradition. The two definitions are interchangeable (paper A's RP309.1 explicitly notes their equivalence).

TP309.2 in paper A states the Indyk-Motwani epsilon-PLEB theorem on the Hamming cube with O(dn + n^{1+1/(1+eps)}) space and O(n^{1/(1+eps)}) hash evaluations per query (cited as external from [31]). TP310.3 in paper B is the canonical LSH theorem: an (r,cr,p1,p2)-sensitive family yields a (c,r)-NN data structure with O(n^rho/p1) query time and O(n^{1+rho}/p1) space, rho=log(1/p1)/log(1/p2). Specializing TP310.3 to Hamming via PrP310.1 yields TP309.2 with c=(1+eps); they are the same result, paper A citing it externally and paper B proving it directly.

AP309.6 is paper A's external description of the Indyk-Motwani PLEB construction: concatenate several LSH function values, reduce ANN to PLEB. AP310.4 is paper B's full description of the LSH near-neighbor data structure: sample L hash functions g_j each a concatenation of k h_i in H, bucket points, scan first 3L candidates on query. They are the same construction, paper A citing what paper B builds explicitly.

Both define the approximate near-neighbor decision problem. ProbP309.1 is paper A's external-cited epsilon-PLEB (Point Location in Equal Balls): given n points in H^d and radius r, on query q report a point at distance <= r(1+eps). DP310.2 is paper B's (c,r)-NN: if D_P(q) <= r, report some p' in B(q,cr). Setting c = 1+eps (and identifying eps-PLEB with (1+eps,r)-NN) makes these the same problem, with Hamming specialized to general metrics in B.

ProbP309.2 (paper A): approximate nearest neighbor in Hamming space, find a (1+eps)-approximate NN for any query q in H^d. DP310.1 (paper B): the c-approximate nearest neighbor problem in metric space (X,D) with failure probability 1-f. The c=(1+eps) ANN problem is identical; paper B is general-metric, paper A restricts to Hamming.

AP309.4 is paper A's 'simple ANN search via random bit permutations': maintain N=O(n^{1/(1+eps)}) sorted orderings of the dataset under random bit permutations, on query binary search and bidirectional scan. This is a Hamming-specific ANN scheme. AP310.4 is paper B's standard LSH bucketing scheme (concatenate k hash functions, sample L, bucket and scan). Both achieve the same asymptotic n^{1/(1+eps)} query time on Hamming via the LSH paradigm, but paper A's bit-permutation version is presented as an alternative implementation that adapts to all radii (RP309.3) whereas paper B's is the canonical bucketed version requiring multiple radii.

Both proofs establish the LSH near-neighbor correctness via the same two events (E1: nearest neighbor collides on at least one of L hash functions; E2: bounded number of far-collisions). PP309.5 (paper A, sketch for the bit-permutation algorithm) uses p1=1-r/d, p2=1-r(1+eps)/d, k=log_{1/p2} n, rho=ln(1/p1)/ln(1/p2), n^rho = O(n^{1/(1+eps)}). PP310.5 (paper B) sets k=ceil(log_{1/p2} n) and L=n^rho/p1 to bound far-collisions and ensure near-collision. Same parameter choices, same probabilistic argument, applied to slightly different data structures.

Composite L2 step alignment for the LSH-correctness proof. Paper A's steps: set parameters p1,p2,k,rho (PSP309.6); bound far-point collisions via p2^k=1/n (PSP309.7); probability nearest neighbor is found is >= 1 - (1-n^{-rho})^{n^rho} > 1/2 (PSP309.8); conclude correctness (PSP309.9). Paper B's steps: bound far collisions with k=log_{1/p2} n giving expected <= L (PSP310.4); apply Markov to get Pr[E2] >= 2/3 (PSP310.5); bound near-collision probability >= p1 n^{-rho} (PSP310.6); choose L=n^rho/p1 to ensure E1 (PSP310.7). Steps are the same probabilistic arithmetic in different orderings; cross-paper L2 alignment is meaningful here because the proof skeletons match exactly.

The random hyperplane hash h_r(u) = sign(r.u) for r ~ Gaussian (DP309.8) and the corresponding SimHash algorithm (AP309.1) are paper A's signature contribution -- the LSH family for cosine/angular similarity. Paper B does not cover angular/cosine LSH at all (its concrete LSH families are coordinate-projection on Hamming PrP310.1 and the l_1 reduction). This is the canonical 'SimHash is the angular specialization of LSH' content that defines the pair name.

TP309.3 (paper A): random hyperplane collision probability Pr[h_r(u)=h_r(v)] = 1 - theta(u,v)/pi. This is the foundational closed-form for SimHash, cited from Goemans-Williamson MAX-CUT. Paper B has no analog: it does not analyze cosine/angular LSH.

Paper A's set-similarity-from-random-hyperplane computation: Pr[h(A)=h(B)] = 1 - theta/pi with theta = arccos(|A cap B|/sqrt(|A||B|)). This is a SimHash-specific consequence (Otsuka-Ochiai/cosine on characteristic vectors). Paper B does not address angular set similarity.

Paper A's structural lemmas about LSH-admitting similarities: LP309.1 (1-sim must satisfy triangle inequality), LP309.2 (binarization to {0,1} hashing), LP309.3 (isometric Hamming embedding). These are paper A's necessary-condition theory of which similarities admit LSH. Paper B does not develop this metric-theoretic side; it works directly with given (r1,r2,p1,p2)-sensitive families.

PrP309.1 (paper A): impossibility result that Dice and Overlap coefficients admit no LSH family because 1-sim violates triangle inequality. Paper B has no impossibility content; the metric-theoretic boundary of LSH is paper A's contribution.

Paper A's EMD content: theorem TP309.1 (LSH for EMD with O(log n log log n) approximation via Kleinberg-Tardos rounding), algorithm AP309.2 (EMD hash via HST + Chekuri-Khanna-Naor-Zosin LP + KT rounding), and the EMD-sketching problem ProbP309.4. Paper B does not address EMD or LP-rounding-based LSH; this is paper A's distinct contribution beyond Hamming/cosine.

Paper A's weighted/continuous min-wise hashing (PrP309.2 collision bound, AP309.3 algorithm via continuous KT rounding, EP309.1 weighted-set collision identity, DP309.10 continuous-set representation S(P)). These extend min-wise to non-negative real weights and have no counterpart in paper B.

Paper A's proofs of its structural lemmas (LP309.1 triangle inequality, LP309.2 binarization, LP309.3 Hamming embedding) and EMD theorem TP309.1. None has a paper B analog because the supporting theorems do not.

OpenP309.1 (paper A): open problem of sketching information-theoretic distances (KL divergence). No paper B analog -- paper B is structured as definitive results on (c,r)-NN data structures, not open problems.

Paper B introduces oblivious vs adaptive randomized correctness models for dynamic NN data structures (DP310.3, DP310.4). Paper A has no analog; the oblivious/adaptive distinction is specific to dynamic data-structure analysis and is paper B's modeling refinement.

Paper B's r_med approximation lemma (LP310.1), connected-components claims (ClP310.1, ClP310.2), and the APPROXIMATE CC algorithm (AP310.1). These are part of paper B's no-preprocessing reduction from approximate-near to approximate-nearest neighbor; paper A does not address this reduction.

Paper B's interval near-neighbor (INearNbr) machinery (LP310.2), point-replication bound (LP310.3), construction-complexity corollary (CP310.1), search-cost claim (ClP310.3), search approximation lemma (LP310.4), and the recursive CONSTRUCT/SEARCH algorithms (AP310.2, AP310.3). All part of paper B's approximate-near to approximate-nearest reduction; paper A has no analog.

Paper B's two main reductions from (c,r)-NN (near neighbor) to c(1+O(gamma))-NN (nearest neighbor): no-preprocessing version TP310.1 and with-preprocessing/adaptive version TP310.2. Paper A does not address this reduction at all.

Paper B's coordinate-range reduction (LP310.5, Bern's trick) and reduction-to-Hamming-cube (LP310.6) for embedding (c,1)-NN over l_1 into Hamming. Paper A does not develop reductions from continuous l_p metrics to Hamming.

Paper B's adaptive-amplification lemma (LP310.7: c log(n+m) independent copies make correctness uniform over all (p,q) pairs) and the resulting adaptive LSH corollary (CP310.2). Paper A has no adaptive-vs-oblivious treatment, so no analog.

Paper B's coordinate-projection LSH for Hamming (PrP310.1: h_i(b1,...,bd) = b_i is (r,rc,1-r/d,1-rc/d)-sensitive), the padding remark (RP310.2), and the calculus claim ClP310.4 used to bound rho<=1/c. Paper A's hyperplane-LSH (DP309.8/AP309.1) is the cosine analog but technically distinct from coordinate-projection on Hamming; the closest content match is PSP309.6 which sets the same parameters p1=1-r/d, p2=1-r(1+eps)/d, but at proof-step level (already aligned above). PrP310.1 itself has no paper-A counterpart at the L1 level.

Paper B's chain of corollaries giving (c,r)-NN over Hamming with n^{1+1/c} space (CP310.3), then over l_1^d via the Hamming reduction (TP310.4), and the further nearest-neighbor versions (CP310.4, CP310.5). Paper A does not chain these particular space/query bounds for l_1; paper A's TP309.2 captures only the Hamming side, already aligned with TP310.3.

Paper B's bucketing approach for (c,r)-NN in l_s^d (TP310.5: O(1/eps)^d space, O(d) query), combined with Johnson-Lindenstrauss to get TP310.6, and the approximate Voronoi diagram TP310.7. These are paper B's curse-of-dimensionality removal route; paper A has no JL or Voronoi content.
Paper B's Geometric MST application: problem ProbP310.1, Kruskal-style algorithm AP310.5, approximation lemma LP310.8, and the resulting MST theorem TP310.9. Paper A does not address MST at all.

Paper B's remark that the conference paper [35] (the original Indyk-Motwani 1998) implicitly assumed p1, p2 bounded away from 0; paper B makes this explicit. This is a self-referential clarification with no paper A counterpart.
